summary: Congestion Exposure (ConEx) lets senders tell the network about congestion their earlier packets met in the same flow. This experimental RFC specifies an IPv6 destination option that carries ConEx markings in IPv6 packets.

eli5.summary: A car showing a sign to the road that says it hit traffic earlier. This defines where on IPv6 packets that sign goes.

questions: what is congestion exposure in ipv6
how does conex help manage traffic
subtitle: Let the network know when your packets hit congestion.

tldr.problem: Networks cannot easily tell which traffic causes congestion and which traffic avoids it. Routers must drop packets blindly during congestion, and audit functions cannot distinguish honest senders from misbehaving ones.
tldr.mechanism: Congestion Exposure (ConEx) marks IPv6 packets with a destination option that tells the network about congestion the packet encountered earlier in the same flow. Four bits signal congestion, loss, credit build-up, and validity of the marking.
tldr.outcome: The protocol is experimental. It enables better traffic management and fairness mechanisms but requires wide deployment to be effective. Adoption in practice has been minimal.

today: RFC 7837 remains Experimental and has not been superseded. It specifies the wire protocol for ConEx in IPv6. RFC 7786 specifies TCP modifications for ConEx. Real-world deployment of ConEx has been minimal; it remains an experimental mechanism that requires coordinated infrastructure changes and has not achieved wide adoption.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Congestion Exposure (ConEx) is a way for senders to tell the network about congestion their packets experienced. This RFC specifies where and how ConEx information goes in IPv6 packets, using a destination option.

A destination option is a piece of optional information that can be included in an IPv6 header. The ConEx Destination Option (CDO) is 2 bytes long and carries four flag bits. Each bit signals something about the packet: whether it is ConEx-capable, whether the sender experienced packet loss, whether Explicit Congestion Notification was seen, or whether the sender is building up credit for future congestion. ConEx is designed for IPv6 only, because IPv4 headers have limited space and middleboxes often strip IPv4 options.
sections.eli5: IPv6 packets can carry extra information in options. ConEx adds a tiny 2-byte option that says: did this packet or earlier packets in the flow hit congestion? This helps the network make smarter decisions about which packets to drop.

sections.title: The ConEx Option Bits
sections.content:
The ConEx Destination Option is 2 bytes: one for the option type (always 0x1E for experimental) and one for the flags. The four flags are:

X (eXposure): Set to 1 if the transport is using ConEx for this packet. If X is 0, the other bits are ignored and must be forwarded unchanged.

L (Loss): Set to 1 if the sender has experienced packet loss in this flow earlier.

E (ECN): Set to 1 if the sender has seen an Explicit Congestion Notification mark, indicating congestion signaled at the IP layer.

C (Credit): Set to 1 if the sender is building up congestion credit, a pre-paid budget to cover potential future losses.

Multiple bits can be set in the same packet. For example, a packet might have both L and C set if the sender experienced loss and is also building credit. When any of L, E, or C is set, the byte count of the packet is counted toward the respective congestion metric. The remaining four bits are reserved for future use and must be set to zero by senders and ignored by receivers.
sections.eli5: Four flags tell the network different things: is ConEx enabled (X), did we lose packets (L), did we see congestion marks (E), and are we saving up credit for later (C)? Routers read these flags and can make smarter decisions.

sections.title: Using ConEx in Practice
sections.content:
ConEx-aware routers must be able to process the ConEx option quickly without slowing down forwarding. To do this, senders SHOULD place the ConEx option as the first destination option in the IPv6 header, before any encryption or authentication headers. This allows ConEx-aware routers to find it without searching through all extension headers.

Non-ConEx-aware routers simply forward the ConEx option unchanged. Since the option type has the "change" bit set to 0, the option is immutable: no router may alter it. IPsec Authentication Headers (AH) can be used to cryptographically verify that the ConEx option has not been modified.

When packets are tunneled through an outer IP header, the ConEx option is normally not copied to the outer header, to avoid double-counting bytes. However, coordinated tunnel implementations MAY copy it to improve visibility for ConEx-aware nodes downstream. At tunnel exit, outer ConEx options should be ignored in favor of the inner ones.
sections.eli5: ConEx-aware routers need to read the option quickly, so senders put it early. Regular routers just pass it along unchanged. If packets are wrapped in an outer layer, you do not copy the marker to avoid counting it twice.

sections.title: Traffic Management and Preferential Drop
sections.content:
Once ConEx information is available in packets, routers can use it to make fairness decisions. One proposed mechanism is preferential drop: when a queue becomes very congested and must drop packets, it can preferentially drop traffic that is not ConEx-marked.

The rationale is that ConEx-marked packets come from senders that are already rate-limited by a ConEx ingress policer, so they are not contributing to the congestion they report. Non-ConEx or unmarked packets are more likely to be from aggressive flows. By dropping unmarked traffic first, the router can mitigate flooding attacks and ensure honest, ConEx-aware senders get better service.

A router implementing preferential drop might use a preference order: drop non-ConEx packets first, then ConEx-capable packets with X bit unset, then ConEx-marked packets (with L, E, or C set). This incentivizes senders to use ConEx and to honestly report congestion.
sections.eli5: When a router is drowning in traffic, it can drop the packets from senders that did not warn about congestion first, and keep the packets from honest senders that are already slowing down.

sections.title: Security and Integrity
sections.content:
A malicious sender could set ConEx bits falsely to trick an audit function into discarding legitimate traffic. To prevent this, the ConEx option should be placed before IPsec encryption so it remains in the clear, and an IPsec Authentication Header can verify its integrity. The option's immutability (chg bit = 0) ensures intermediate nodes cannot alter it.

The four reserved bits in the ConEx option could theoretically be used as a covert channel to send information outside the control of IPsec encryption. However, this is only a concern if the covert channel can bypass IPsec in tunnel mode. In transport mode, the reserved bits are outside the encrypted payload, but in tunnel mode, ESP encryption would close the channel.

One design trade-off is that ConEx is encoded as a destination option, which means it can be encapsulated by tunnel headers and thus hidden from downstream ConEx-aware nodes. The specification accepts this limitation in order to avoid the performance penalty of hop-by-hop options (which all intermediate nodes must examine).
sections.eli5: A liar could set the ConEx bits to fool routers. IPsec can prevent this by signing the option so nobody can change it. If someone tunnels a packet, the inner ConEx marking is what counts, not the outer one.

sections.title: Status and Experimentation
sections.content:
RFC 7837 defines an Experimental protocol. The ConEx working group chose the destination option encoding as a compromise between competing requirements: it is visible to ConEx-aware routers, can be forwarded unchanged by regular routers, and does not impose processing on the fast path of non-ConEx-aware nodes.

The experiment is expected to last at least two years from publication to allow infrastructure and IPv6 deployment to mature. Evaluating ConEx requires real IPv6 traffic and deployment of ConEx-aware routers, which takes time. As of 2016, ConEx has seen limited real-world deployment, and it remains an experimental protocol without plans for progression to Standards Track.
sections.eli5: This is an experimental idea to test whether networks can use these markings to manage congestion fairly. It has not been widely adopted yet, so it remains in experimental status.
